intro: In 1913, Arthur Nikisch and the Berlin Philharmonic play Beethoven’s Fifth into a recording horn. The omitted exposition repeat takes the first movement straight from its E♭-major song into the development, where the familiar rhythm begins to break apart.

sections.label: A · The opening in bare octaves
sections.mNote: Three short notes fall into a fermata

sections.label: B · The horns call towards E♭
sections.mNote: A sweet violin melody follows the horn call

sections.label: C · The horns change their ending
sections.mNote: The development begins; D♭ in the strings clashes with G

sections.label: D · Diminished chords before the opening returns
sections.mNote: Quiet wind and string replies lead back to C minor

sections.label: E · C-major cadences lead into the coda
sections.mNote: The long closing passage eventually restores C minor

cues.title: Two pauses in five bars
cues.text: Three Gs fall to E♭; three Fs fall to D. Each long note has a fermata, giving Nikisch room to hold the orchestra still. The second hold lasts across two written bars.
cues.evidence: Beethoven, Symphony No. 5, I, bars 1–5; Mutopia 941, first-violin and cello parts.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: An orchestra before a horn
cues.text: On 10 November 1913, Nikisch and the Berlin Philharmonic record the whole symphony in one day. Engineer Max Hampe captures their playing through a horn: air moves a diaphragm, and a stylus cuts the music into wax.
cues.evidence: Aleks Kolkowski, Duncan Miller and Amy Blier-Carruthers, ‘The art and science of acoustic recording’, Science Museum Group Journal, 2015: session, engineer and acoustic recording process. https://journal.sciencemuseum.ac.uk/article/acoustic-recording/

cues.title: Horns before the violin song
cues.text: The horns stretch the opening rhythm into a call across wider intervals. Their last B♭ stays beneath the violin melody, which begins softly in E♭ major. The cellos keep the repeated notes moving under the song.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 59–70; Mutopia 941, horns, first violin and cello.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Straight into the development
cues.text: Nikisch leaves out the exposition repeat. After the E♭-major cadence, the horns’ three B♭s fall to G; the strings answer D♭–D♭–D♭–C. That clash begins the development immediately.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 125–128; Mutopia 941. The omitted repeat is documented by Kolkowski, Miller and Blier-Carruthers: https://journal.sciencemuseum.ac.uk/article/acoustic-recording/.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The opening with reinforcements
cues.text: G–G–G–E♭ returns, with winds and horns reinforcing the strings. Beethoven has rebuilt the opening out of short fragments and quiet chord exchanges. The fermatas stop the orchestra again.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 233–253; Mutopia 941, strings, oboes and horns. The recapitulation begins at 248.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: One oboe remains
cues.text: A G-major chord stops the orchestra, but the oboe keeps its note. Alone, it descends F–E♭–D, adds a little turn and descends again. Beethoven writes Adagio over this tiny solo inside the Allegro.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bar 268; Mutopia 941, oboe part and string rests.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: Bassoons take the horn call
cues.text: The bassoons inherit the horn call, now G–G–G–C–D–G. The violin melody follows in C major. Its first leap, G up to C, keeps the familiar shape while bringing the song closer to the home key.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 303–310; Mutopia 941, bassoon and first-violin parts; compare 59–66.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

cues.title: The bass shifts under C
cues.text: The violins stay high on C while the bass moves C–A♭–E–F. Those changing foundations keep the cadence from settling. The coda has a long way to go before its closing C-minor chords.
cues.evidence: Symphony No. 5, I, bars 374–381 and 491–502; Mutopia 941, string parts.
cues.how: Timed from the score, aligned to this recording automatically.

composer.epithet: He could make a symphony out of four notes, and spent his last years finding things four string players had never said.
facts: Neefe in Bonn; Haydn, Albrechtsberger and Salieri in Vienna
Bonn until 1792; Vienna and its surrounding villages for the rest of his life
Nine symphonies · five numbered piano concertos · 32 numbered piano sonatas · 16 string quartets · Fidelio
Described his hearing loss in 1801; used conversation books from 1818

quote.text: I live only in my notes.
quote.source: Beethoven to Franz Gerhard Wegeler, Vienna, 29 June 1801; our translation

composer.background:
In March 1778 Johann van Beethoven advertised a concert in Cologne by his six-year-old son. Ludwig was seven. His father, a singer in the electoral chapel at Bonn, hoped to launch another child prodigy; his grandfather, also Ludwig, had risen from singer to Kapellmeister in the same establishment. The boy was baptised on 17 December 1770, probably the day after his birth. Music was the family trade. By his teens he was playing the organ for services and the viola in the court orchestra, learning operas from the middle of the string section.

Christian Gottlob Neefe put Bach’s Well-Tempered Clavier before him and helped him into paid employment. The Breuning household supplied books, friendship and a refuge from Johann’s drinking. After his mother died in 1787, Beethoven increasingly supported his younger brothers. In November 1792 the elector sent him to Vienna to study with Haydn. He was supposed to come back. French troops occupied Bonn in 1794, and the court that paid him disappeared.
